deep.reconstruction:
Problem (stated on the previous page): for a prime P = 4n+1, find all a with P | a^2+1. Euler first writes P = p^2+q^2. By his lemma on divisors of sums of two squares, any solution a, b of P | a^2+b^2 has the form a = pr+qs, b = ps−qr. With b = ±1 this requires ps−qr = ±1, so r/s is a fraction 'next to' p/q.

This page supplies the construction. Run the Euclidean algorithm on p and q and form the continued-fraction convergents. The last convergent is p/q and the penultimate one can be taken as r/s, so that ps−qr = ±1. This is possible because gcd(p,q)=1; otherwise their common factor squared would divide P, contradicting primality.

The identity (pr+qs)^2 + (ps−qr)^2 = (p^2+q^2)(r^2+s^2) then gives a^2+1 = P(r^2+s^2) for a = pr+qs. So a is a square root of −1 mod P.

Replacing r/s by (mp+r)/(mq+s) keeps the cross-product difference ±1, since the cross products are mpq+ps and mpq+qr. It changes a into a + mP. Allowing r, s to be negative gives the sign, so a = mP ± (pr+qs). These are all the solutions, since x^2 ≡ −1 has exactly two roots mod a prime.

In modern terms, a ≡ ∓p·q^{-1} (mod P). Euler is computing a modular inverse by the extended Euclidean algorithm, starting from the two-square representation.

Example 1 begins: 29 = 5^2+2^2, so p=5, q=2. The next page gives convergents 2/1 and 5/2, hence a = 10+2 = 12 and a ≡ ±12 (mod 29). Check: 145 = 5·29.
errors: None. Cross products, the gcd argument and the general solution a = m(4n+1) ± (pr+qs) are all correct. The sign of ps−qr may be +1 or −1 depending on the parity of the convergent index, but Euler allows ±, so this is harmless.

ideas.what: Using the penultimate continued-fraction convergent of p/q to obtain ps−qr = ±1 (Bézout coefficients via the Euclidean algorithm).
ideas.modern_name: Extended Euclidean algorithm / convergents of continued fractions
ideas.usually_credited_to: Bachet (1621) for the linear Diophantine use; Huygens and Wallis for convergent properties
ideas.where_published: Euler's earlier arithmetic papers on linear indeterminate problems (he says 'alio loco ostendi'). The exact paper is unsure, possibly E36.

ideas.what: Square root of −1 mod a prime p^2+q^2 obtained as pr+qs, via the Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity.
ideas.modern_name: Computing sqrt(−1) mod P from a two-square representation (≡ p·q^{-1})
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore; the reverse direction (from sqrt(−1) to p, q) is due to Hermite and Serret (1848), Smith (1855) and Cornacchia (1908)
ideas.where_published: This paper E283 (Novi Commentarii 9, 1764); it relies on Euler's two-squares divisor theorem (E241 and related).

ideas.what: Parametrising all convergent-neighbours (mp+r)/(mq+s) to obtain the full residue class of solutions.
ideas.modern_name: Solutions of a linear congruence form a residue class / unimodular matrices

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but routine application of the Euclidean algorithm and the two-squares identity. Its direction (from the two-square representation to sqrt(−1)) is the easy one, and it is well documented in Euler's number-theory papers.
transcription_corrections: No substantive errors. The image matches the transcription; the long s ('ſ') is retained in the transcription.
